passages.t: Morning, and the end of Judas
passages.happening:
When morning comes, the chief priests and elders make their decision to put Jesus to death. They tie him up, lead him away, and hand him over to Pilate the governor.

When Judas sees that Jesus has been condemned, he is filled with remorse. He takes the thirty pieces of silver back to the chief priests and elders. “I have sinned by betraying innocent blood,” he says (verse 4). “What is that to us?” they reply. “You bear the responsibility.” Judas throws the silver into the temple and leaves. Then he goes away and hangs himself (verse 5).

The chief priests pick up the silver. They say it is against the law to put it in the temple treasury, because it is blood money. So they use it to buy the potter's field as a burial place for foreigners. That is why it is called the Field of Blood to this day. Matthew says this fulfilled what was spoken through Jeremiah the prophet: “They took the thirty pieces of silver, the price set on Him by the people of Israel, and they gave them for the potter’s field, as the Lord had commanded me” (verses 9-10).
passages.hearers:
Only Matthew tells this part of Judas's story. He tells Judas's death in a few words and does not linger on it, and these notes will not either.

Notice what Judas says. He calls Jesus ‘innocent blood’. Judas is the first person in the passion story to say out loud that Jesus is innocent. Pilate's wife will say it next (verse 19).

Notice too what the priests say: ‘You bear the responsibility.’ Pilate will use the very same words to the crowd (verse 24). In this chapter everyone tries to hand the guilt to someone else. The priests are careful about the law of the treasury, and careless about the innocent man.

‘Blood money’ means money paid for a death. A burial ground for foreigners would be for pilgrims and strangers who died in Jerusalem far from home. The priests do not want the coins in God's treasury, yet the money ends up buying a place of rest for outsiders.
passages.ot:
Matthew's quotation joins more than one passage. The words about thirty pieces of silver come from Zechariah, where the shepherd is paid a slave's price and God tells him to throw it “to the potter in the house of the LORD” (Zechariah 11:13). The potter and the field recall Jeremiah. God sent Jeremiah to buy a clay jar from a potter and to smash it in the Valley of Ben-hinnom as a sign of judgment (Jeremiah 19:1-2, 11). Later Jeremiah bought a field and “weighed out seventeen shekels of silver” (Jeremiah 32:9).

Some readers also notice an older story. When David's trusted adviser Ahithophel turned against him and his plan failed, he went home and “hanged himself” (2 Samuel 17:23). The betrayer of David's son ends the same way.
passages.hard:
Why does Matthew say Jeremiah when the words about the silver are mostly from Zechariah? Christians have given several answers. Many scholars think Matthew blended passages from both prophets and named the more famous one, Jeremiah, whose potter, field and valley of judgment give the scene its setting. Some note that Matthew says ‘spoken through’ Jeremiah, not ‘written’. A few think Matthew simply made a slip. The earliest manuscripts all read ‘Jeremiah’. These notes do not choose.

How did Judas die? Acts gives a different account of his death and of the field (Acts 1:18-19). There Judas himself buys the field with his reward, and his death happens there. Christians have answered in different ways. Some think the two accounts tell two stages of one event. Some think the priests bought the field in Judas's name, since it was his money. Others think the early church remembered the main facts, that Judas died soon after and that a field called the Field of Blood was tied to him, and told the details in two ways. These notes do not choose. Both accounts agree that Judas came to a terrible end and that the field was linked to the blood money.

Matthew tells Judas's death in one plain sentence. Many people carry shame for something they have done, and some have thought of ending their life. If that is you, please do not carry it alone. Tell God, and tell someone near you: a friend, a pastor, a doctor. If you have thought of ending your life, please reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service where you live. The priests could only say, ‘You bear the responsibility.’ They had no mercy to give. Jesus, whose blood was poured out “for the forgiveness of sins” (26:28), is the one to bring any guilt to. These notes do not say what God did with Judas. That belongs to God.
passages.asks: Judas and Peter both failed Jesus on the same night, and both were full of sorrow. Peter wept, and he is found among the eleven again on the mountain in Galilee (28:16). Judas went to the priests, who turned him away. Ask where you take your guilt: to people who say ‘that is your problem’, or to the one whose blood was poured out for forgiveness. No failure is too large to bring to him.

passages.happening: Jesus stands before the governor. Pilate asks him, “Are You the King of the Jews?” Jesus replies, “You have said so” (verse 11). The chief priests and elders accuse him, and he gives no answer. Pilate asks, “Do You not hear how many charges they are bringing against You?” (verse 13). But Jesus does not answer a single charge, and the governor is amazed.
passages.hearers:
Mark tells this too (Mark 15:1-5), and the note on Mark 15 explains it. Pontius Pilate governed Judea for Rome from about AD 26 to 36. A stone found at Caesarea in 1961 calls him ‘prefect of Judea’. The Roman historian Tacitus, writing around AD 116, says that Christ was executed in the reign of Tiberius by Pontius Pilate (Annals 15.44).

The Jewish historian Josephus also has a short passage about Jesus. Christian copyists later added to it, but most scholars think Josephus himself wrote that Pilate condemned Jesus to the cross after leading men among the Jews accused him (Antiquities 18.63-64). The Gospels and these outside writers agree on the main fact: Jesus was put to death on the order of the Roman governor.

Notice how the question has changed. Before the council the issue was whether Jesus was the Christ, the Son of God. Before Pilate it is whether he is ‘King of the Jews’. To Rome, a man claiming to be a king was a rebel against Caesar.

Matthew calls Pilate simply ‘the governor’ again and again. The note on Mark 15 explains why the sentence was Pilate's: crucifixion was a Roman punishment, carried out under a Roman governor's authority.
passages.ot:
Jesus' silence recalls Isaiah's servant: “He was oppressed and afflicted, yet He did not open His mouth” (Isaiah 53:7).

Long before, Jesus had told his disciples that he would be handed over to the Gentiles to be mocked and flogged and crucified (20:19). The Psalms had asked why “the kings of the earth take their stand and the rulers gather together, against the LORD and against His Anointed One” (Psalm 2:2).
passages.hard: Why does Jesus refuse to answer? He has already told the truth under oath before the high priest (26:64), and he gives Pilate a short reply. To the rest he says nothing. Some think he would not dignify false charges. Others see the servant of Isaiah 53, who goes to his death without protest. Many think both. His silence is not weakness. Pilate, who holds all the power in the room, is the one left amazed.
passages.asks: Jesus says very little before Pilate. He does not plead or argue. Ask what it means that the King of all things stood silent in a governor's court. There is a strength in not needing to win every argument. There is also a cost in telling the truth to power, and Jesus paid it.

passages.t: Barabbas, a dream, washed hands, and the crowd's cry
passages.happening:
At the feast it was the governor's custom to release one prisoner the crowd chose. A notorious prisoner named Barabbas was being held. Pilate asks the crowd, “Which one do you want me to release to you: Barabbas, or Jesus who is called Christ?” (verse 17). He knows the leaders handed Jesus over out of envy.

While Pilate is sitting on the judgment seat, his wife sends him a message: “Have nothing to do with that innocent man, for I have suffered terribly in a dream today because of Him” (verse 19).

But the chief priests and elders persuade the crowds to ask for Barabbas and to have Jesus put to death. Pilate asks what he should do with Jesus. They all answer, “Crucify Him!” “Why?” asks Pilate. “What evil has He done?” But they shout all the louder.

Pilate sees he is getting nowhere and that a riot is starting. He takes water and washes his hands in front of the crowd. “I am innocent of this man’s blood,” he says. “You bear the responsibility” (verse 24). All the people answer, “His blood be on us and on our children!” (verse 25). Pilate releases Barabbas, has Jesus flogged, and hands him over to be crucified.
passages.hearers:
Mark tells of Barabbas too (Mark 15:6-15), and the note on Mark 15 explains the custom of release, Barabbas's name, which means ‘son of the father’, and the Roman flogging. Matthew adds three things: the dream, the washed hands, and the cry of verse 25.

Only Matthew tells of Pilate's wife. God speaks through dreams at the start of Matthew's Gospel, to Joseph and to the wise men from the east (1:20; 2:12). Now he speaks again in a dream, and this time to a Roman woman. She calls Jesus ‘that innocent man’. The Gospel does not give her name. Later Christian tradition called her Procula, and the Orthodox and Ethiopian churches honour her as a saint. Origen, in the early third century, thought the dream was meant to turn her toward Christ.

Washing the hands was a sign everyone understood. The law of Moses had a rite for an unsolved murder in which the elders washed their hands and said, “Our hands did not shed this blood” (Deuteronomy 21:7). Pilate uses the gesture to say the death is not his doing. Matthew lets the reader see the truth. Pilate had the power to free Jesus. He chose not to. Water could not wash that away.

The crowd's answer uses an old formula of the Old Testament for accepting the blame for a death. Joshua's spies told Rahab that anyone who left her house would have his blood “on his own head” (Joshua 2:19). It was a way of saying, ‘we take the responsibility’.
passages.ot:
The formula appears in many places. David said to the man who claimed to have killed Saul, “Your blood be on your own head” (2 Samuel 1:16). Jeremiah warned the leaders of his day that if they killed him they would “bring innocent blood upon yourselves” (Jeremiah 26:15).

But the law of Moses also limits such words. “Fathers shall not be put to death for their children, nor children for their fathers; each is to die for his own sin” (Deuteronomy 24:16). No crowd can place guilt on children not yet born.

Isaiah's servant was “numbered with the transgressors” (Isaiah 53:12). A guilty man walks free and an innocent one is condemned.
passages.hard:
“His blood be on us and on our children” (verse 25) is the most misused sentence in the New Testament. In the story it is the cry of one crowd, in one city, on one morning, stirred up by its leaders (verse 20). It is a legal formula for taking responsibility for a death. Scripture itself forbids putting the guilt of fathers on their children (Deuteronomy 24:16). And Matthew has already told his readers what Jesus' blood is for. On the night before, Jesus said his blood is “poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins” (26:28). Many readers think Matthew wants us to hear the terrible irony: the crowd calls down the very blood that was shed to forgive. Historians debate how much the conflict between Matthew's church and synagogue leaders shaped this scene. That debate does not change what the verse may and may not be used to say.

For centuries many Christians called the Jewish people ‘Christ-killers’ and used scenes like this to justify contempt, expulsions, and violence against Jews. Passion plays spoke this line aloud as if it were a curse on the Jewish people for all time. That reading is false, and Christians must reject it plainly. This site rejects it. Jesus himself, his disciples, and the crowds who welcomed him were Jews. A Roman governor gave the order, and Roman soldiers carried it out. In 1965 the Catholic Church's Second Vatican Council said that what happened in the passion ‘cannot be charged against all the Jews, without distinction, then alive, nor against the Jews of today’. Most churches teach the same. The New Testament places all people inside the guilt: in Acts the first Christians pray that Herod, Pilate, the Gentiles, and the people of Israel all stood together against Jesus (Acts 4:27).

Was there really a custom of releasing a prisoner at Passover? No record of it has been found outside the Gospels. The note on Mark 15 sets out the views and leaves the question open.
passages.asks: Everyone in this scene tries to pass the blame. The priests to Judas. Pilate to the crowd. The crowd to itself and its children. Only Jesus, who is innocent, carries it. Ask where you are tempted to wash your hands of something you could have stopped. And ask whether you see yourself in Barabbas: someone set free by the death of another.

passages.happening: The governor's soldiers take Jesus into the Praetorium, the governor's headquarters, and gather the whole company around him. They strip him and put a scarlet robe on him. They twist a crown out of thorns and set it on his head, put a staff in his right hand, and kneel in front of him, mocking: “Hail, King of the Jews!” (verse 29). They spit on him and hit him on the head with the staff again and again. Then they take off the robe, put his own clothes back on him, and lead him away to be crucified.
passages.hearers:
Mark tells this too (Mark 15:16-20), and the note on Mark 15 explains it. The soldiers are acting out a coronation as a cruel joke. A robe, a crown, a sceptre and kneeling were how people honoured a ruler.

Matthew's details differ a little. In Mark the robe is purple, the colour of kings. In Matthew it is scarlet, and Matthew alone mentions the staff in the right hand, held like a sceptre.

These were the governor's soldiers. The great irony is that every part of the joke is true. The man in the robe really is the king.
passages.ot: Isaiah's servant says, “I offered My back to those who struck Me,” and “I did not hide My face from scorn and spittle” (Isaiah 50:6). Jesus had said in 20:19 that the Gentiles would mock him, flog him and crucify him.
passages.hard: Why does Matthew describe the mocking in such detail, but say almost nothing of the pain of crucifixion? Like Mark, Matthew seems more interested in what the scene means than in how it felt. He shows the world's view of Jesus as a fake king, so that the reader can see the truth underneath. It is wise to follow Matthew here and not to linger on the cruelty for its own sake.
passages.asks: The soldiers knelt to Jesus as a joke. Ask whether there are ways you give Jesus the outward signs of honour without meaning them. Jesus let himself be made a fool of by men he could have destroyed. That is what his kind of kingship looks like.

passages.happening:
On the way out the soldiers find a man from Cyrene named Simon and force him to carry Jesus' cross. They come to a place called Golgotha, which means the Place of the Skull. They offer Jesus wine mixed with gall. He tastes it and refuses to drink. They crucify him and divide his clothes by casting lots, and they sit down and keep watch over him. Above his head they post the charge: THIS IS JESUS, THE KING OF THE JEWS. Two robbers are crucified with him, one on each side.

People passing by shake their heads and jeer: “If You are the Son of God, come down from the cross!” (verse 40). The chief priests, scribes and elders mock him too: “He saved others, but He cannot save Himself” (verse 42). “He trusts in God. Let God deliver Him now if He wants Him” (verse 43). Even the robbers crucified with him insult him.
passages.hearers:
Mark tells this too (Mark 15:21-32), and the note on Mark 15 explains crucifixion: a Roman punishment for slaves, rebels and violent criminals, meant to be slow, public and shameful. Like Mark, Matthew tells none of the physical details. He simply writes, “When they had crucified Him” (verse 35). His first hearers knew what that meant.

Matthew adds a few things. The soldiers ‘kept watch’ over him. So the soldiers were there throughout, and they will see what happens at his death (verse 54).

The mockers' words sound familiar to a reader of Matthew. ‘If You are the Son of God’ is what the devil said in the wilderness: “If You are the Son of God, tell these stones to become bread” (4:3). The test is the same as at the start. Jesus could save himself. He refuses, again.

Only Matthew has the mockers say, ‘He trusts in God. Let God deliver Him now.’ They are, without knowing it, quoting a psalm.
passages.ot:
Psalm 22 runs all through this scene. “They divide my garments among them and cast lots for my clothing” (Psalm 22:18). “All who see me mock me; they sneer and shake their heads” (Psalm 22:7). And the leaders' taunt is almost word for word the psalm: “He trusts in the LORD, let the LORD deliver him; let the LORD rescue him, since He delights in him” (Psalm 22:8).

The wine mixed with gall recalls another psalm of a righteous sufferer: “They poisoned my food with gall and gave me vinegar to quench my thirst” (Psalm 69:21).
passages.hard:
The mockers say, ‘He saved others, but He cannot save Himself.’ They mean it as an insult. Matthew means it as the truth. Jesus had said that whoever wants to save his life will lose it (16:25), and that he came to give his life as a ransom for many (20:28). He does not come down from the cross, not because he cannot, but because staying there is how he saves others.

Why does he refuse the drink? Mark says it was wine mixed with myrrh, and many think it was offered to dull the pain. Matthew calls it gall, a bitter thing, to echo Psalm 69. Jesus tastes it and refuses. Many think he chose to face what was coming with a clear mind.
passages.asks: Simon was a stranger passing by, and he ended up carrying the cross of Jesus. Ask what crosses have been put on your shoulders that you did not choose, and whether they might also bring you nearer to Jesus. And notice who is mocking: the passersby, the leaders, and even the dying men next to him. Matthew leaves no group outside.

passages.happening: From noon until three in the afternoon darkness comes over all the land. About three o'clock Jesus cries out in a loud voice, “Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani?” which means, “My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?” (verse 46). Some who hear him say, “He is calling Elijah.” One of them runs, fills a sponge with sour wine, puts it on a reed and holds it up for him to drink. The others say, “Leave Him alone. Let us see if Elijah comes to save Him” (verse 49). Jesus cries out again in a loud voice and yields up his spirit.
passages.hearers:
Mark tells this too (Mark 15:33-37), and the note on Mark 15 explains the hours, the sour wine and the hope that Elijah would come. Many Jews believed Elijah would come again before the day of the Lord (Malachi 4:5).

Mark has ‘Eloi’, the Aramaic form. Matthew has ‘Eli’, which is closer to the Hebrew of the psalm. Some think Matthew made the words match the psalm his readers knew. Others think ‘Eli’ makes it easier to see how bystanders could mishear the name Elijah. The rest of the cry is Aramaic in both.

Matthew says Jesus ‘yielded up His spirit’. It sounds like an act of his own. He was not simply overpowered by death. He gave up his life.
passages.ot:
Jesus' cry is the first line of Psalm 22: “My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?” The psalm begins in the depths, but it does not end there. It turns to trust: “He has not hidden His face from him, but has attended to his cry for help” (Psalm 22:24). It ends with the nations turning to God: “All the ends of the earth will remember and turn to the LORD” (Psalm 22:27).

The darkness recalls Amos: “I will make the sun go down at noon, and I will darken the earth in the daytime” (Amos 8:9).
passages.hard:
Was Jesus truly abandoned by God? Christians have read the cry in several ways.

Some stress that Jesus is praying a psalm. A psalm's first line could call the whole psalm to mind, and Psalm 22 ends in trust and victory. So the cry is faith spoken from the depths, not despair.

Others insist that the first line must be heard in its full force. Jesus felt real abandonment and did not pretend otherwise. Many connect this with Paul's words that God “made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf” (2 Corinthians 5:21): Jesus bore the judgment due to sin, including the loss of the felt presence of God.

Others say that Jesus spoke for the whole human race he had joined, voicing our forsakenness as his own.

These readings can overlap, and Christians who share the faith of the creeds hold them in different blends. Even in the cry, Jesus still calls God ‘my God’. These notes do not settle how best to describe what the Son went through.

The cry also speaks to anyone who has felt forsaken by God. Jesus did not hide that feeling. He took it to God in the words of Scripture. If you feel that way, you can pray it too, and you should not stay alone with it. Tell someone you trust, and if you are in danger, reach out for help today.
passages.asks: Jesus prayed a psalm in his worst hour. When he had no words of his own, he used the words Scripture gave him. Ask whether you have words to pray when you feel abandoned. And if you have ever prayed ‘why have You forsaken me?’, notice that Jesus prayed it first.

passages.t: The curtain torn, the earth shaken, the tombs opened
passages.happening:
At that moment the veil of the temple is torn in two from top to bottom. The earth quakes and the rocks split. The tombs break open, and the bodies of many saints who had fallen asleep are raised. After Jesus' resurrection they come out of the tombs, go into the holy city, and appear to many people.

The centurion and those with him who were guarding Jesus see the earthquake and all that has happened. They are terrified and say, “Truly this was the Son of God” (verse 54).

Many women are there, watching from a distance. They had followed Jesus from Galilee to care for him. Among them are Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joseph, and the mother of Zebedee's sons.
passages.hearers:
Mark tells of the torn curtain and the centurion too (Mark 15:38-41), and the note on Mark 15 explains the temple curtains and the centurion, a Roman officer who commanded a company of soldiers.

Only Matthew tells of the earthquake, the split rocks and the raised saints. ‘Fallen asleep’ was a gentle way of speaking of the dead, used by Jews and by the first Christians. ‘The holy city’ is Jerusalem.

In Mark the centurion speaks alone. In Matthew it is the centurion and the soldiers with him, the same men who kept watch at the cross (verse 36). Gentile soldiers, men like those who had mocked him that morning, are the first in Matthew's passion story to confess him. Earlier in the Gospel the disciples in the boat had said, “Truly You are the Son of God!” (14:33). Now Roman soldiers say it at the cross.

The women had followed Jesus all along. The men have run away. The women stay. One of them is the mother of James and John, who once asked Jesus for places of honour for her sons at his right and left (20:20-21). Now she sees who is on his right and left: two robbers.
passages.ot:
The raised saints recall Ezekiel's vision of the valley of dry bones, where God says, “O My people, I will open your graves and bring you up from them” (Ezekiel 37:12). Isaiah had hoped, “Your dead will live; their bodies will rise” (Isaiah 26:19), and Daniel saw that “many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake” (Daniel 12:2).

The veil in the tabernacle hung before the Most Holy Place: “the veil will separate the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place” (Exodus 26:33).
passages.hard:
What about the raised saints? Only Matthew tells of them, and no other ancient writer mentions such an event. Christians have read verses 52 and 53 in more than one way. Many read them as a real event: God raised some of the faithful dead as a sign that Jesus' death had broken death's hold. Matthew carefully says they came out ‘after Jesus' resurrection’, so that Jesus is still the first to rise. Others, including some who hold a high view of Scripture, read the verses as picture-language of the kind the prophets used, showing what the death of Jesus means: the graves of God's people are opened, as Ezekiel promised. Skeptics ask why, if many dead people walked into Jerusalem, no one else recorded it. Those who read it as an event reply that much in ancient history is known from only one source, and that Matthew does not say how many came or how long they stayed. These notes do not choose. All agree on Matthew's point: the death of Jesus is the beginning of the end of death.

Why was the curtain torn? Some read it as a sign that the way into God's presence is now open, as the letter to the Hebrews says, “the new and living way opened for us through the curtain of His body” (Hebrews 10:20). Others read it as a sign of judgment on the temple, which Jesus had said would fall (24:2). Many hold both.
passages.asks: The first people in Matthew's passion story to call Jesus the Son of God after his death were Roman soldiers who had just crucified him. Ask who you think is too far away from God to see him. And notice the women. They could do nothing to stop what happened. They could only stay and watch. Sometimes faithfulness looks like that.

passages.happening: When evening comes, a rich man from Arimathea named Joseph, who was himself a disciple of Jesus, goes to Pilate and asks for the body. Pilate orders that it be given to him. Joseph takes the body, wraps it in a clean linen cloth, and places it in his own new tomb, which he had cut into the rock. He rolls a great stone across the entrance and goes away. Mary Magdalene and the other Mary are sitting there, opposite the tomb.
passages.hearers:
Mark tells this too (Mark 15:42-47), and the note on Mark 15 explains the burial. The law said the body of an executed man must not be left hanging overnight (Deuteronomy 21:23), so the burial had to be done before the Sabbath began at sunset.

Matthew adds that Joseph was rich, that he was a disciple of Jesus, and that the tomb was his own and new. No one else had been laid in it. Wealthier families cut tombs into the rock outside the city, and a large stone closed the entrance.

Matthew is careful to say that two women sat facing the tomb. They saw where he was laid. They will come back to the same tomb on Sunday morning.
passages.ot:
Isaiah's servant “was assigned a grave with the wicked, and with a rich man in His death” (Isaiah 53:9). Jesus dies between two robbers and is buried in a rich man's tomb.

The law said, “you must not leave the body on the tree overnight, but you must be sure to bury him that day” (Deuteronomy 21:23). Joseph keeps that law for Jesus.
passages.hard: Did Jesus really die, or did he only faint? Matthew, like Mark, takes care to show that he died. The soldiers who kept watch saw him die. Joseph wrapped the body and closed the tomb with a great stone. The women watched. And in the next passage the chief priests themselves treat him as dead and buried. In Matthew's account there is no doubt: Jesus was dead.
passages.asks: Joseph was a rich man and a disciple. John says he had been a disciple in secret (John 19:38). At the darkest moment he stepped forward and gave his own tomb. Ask what it would mean for you to step out of the background for Jesus, even when it seems everything is lost.

passages.happening:
The next day, the day after Preparation Day, which was the Sabbath, the chief priests and Pharisees go to Pilate. “Sir,” they say, “we remember that while He was alive that deceiver said, ‘After three days I will rise again’” (verse 63). They ask him to order the tomb to be made secure until the third day, so that his disciples cannot come and steal the body and tell the people he has risen from the dead. “And this last deception would be worse than the first” (verse 64).

“You have a guard,” Pilate answers. “Go, make the tomb as secure as you know how” (verse 65). So they go and secure the tomb by sealing the stone and posting the guard.
passages.hearers:
Only Matthew tells of the guard. Preparation Day was the Friday, the day before the Sabbath (Mark 15:42). So this is the Saturday.

‘You have a guard’ can be read two ways in the Greek. It may mean ‘take a guard of Roman soldiers’, or ‘you have your own guard’, the temple police. In the next chapter the guards report to the chief priests (28:11), and the priests promise to keep them out of trouble with the governor (28:14). Readers differ on which kind of guard Matthew means.

A seal was a cord or clay stamp across the stone. If it was broken, everyone would know the tomb had been opened.

The leaders remember what Jesus said about rising after three days. Jesus had said it more than once (12:40; 16:21). The disciples seem to have forgotten. His enemies have not.
passages.ot:
Jesus had pointed to Jonah: “as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so the Son of Man will be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth” (12:40, recalling Jonah 1:17). The leaders take that sign seriously enough to post a guard.

The Psalms speak of rulers who plot against the LORD and his anointed, and of God who “laughs” at them from heaven (Psalm 2:4). Stone, seal and soldiers will not hold what God means to open.
passages.hard:
Was there really a guard? Skeptics make a serious case. Only Matthew tells it. Many scholars think it was told to answer the charge, known to Matthew (28:15), that the disciples stole the body. Some ask why the guard was posted only on the Saturday, leaving the tomb unwatched on Friday night.

Those who think the story is history reply in several ways. Many events in ancient history are known from only one source, and that alone does not make them false. Matthew is open about the rumour he is answering, and the rumour itself agrees that the tomb was empty; the argument was over how. The leaders may have checked the tomb before setting the seal. A later writing, the Gospel of Peter, also tells of guards at the tomb, though scholars debate whether it simply borrowed from Matthew. These notes set out both sides and do not choose. The resurrection does not rest on this passage alone. Paul, writing in the 50s, lists witnesses who saw the risen Jesus (1 Corinthians 15:3-8).
passages.asks: The leaders did everything they could to keep Jesus in the grave: a stone, a seal and a guard. Ask what you have tried to seal shut, in your own life, that God may mean to open. And notice the honest question underneath this passage: could the body have been stolen? Matthew does not avoid it. Neither should anyone who wants to know whether Jesus rose.
